title: Image tensors and channels
goals: Read a pixel using declared row column and channel axes
Convert channel layout without changing pixel meaning
Distinguish fixed value scaling from information losing transformations
vocabulary: A numerical array with a declared set of axes
One component plane of an image such as red green or blue
The sequence of meanings assigned to array dimensions
A declared numerical conversion applied to stored values

blocks.title: The same pixels in three channel planes
blocks.caption: Each row describes one channel plane. Within a plane the first listed row is the image top and the second is the bottom. Combining the three values at the same position recovers its RGB triplet.

blocks.label: Use the planes to reconstruct the top-right and bottom-right RGB pixels. Give both HWC and CHW indices for the top-right green value.

guided_practice.title: Audit an axis conversion
guided_practice.prompt: A program flattens the lesson HWC array and groups the first four values into a 2 by 2 red plane. Give that incorrect plane and the correct plane. Identify a position where they disagree.
guided_practice.answer: Teacher explanation: The incorrect plane is [[255, 0], [0, 0]]. The correct red plane is [[255, 0], [0, 255]]. They disagree at row 1 column 1. Regrouping consecutive values does not transpose axes.

independent_case.title: Convert a new image independently
independent_case.task: A one-row two-column RGB image has pixels [10, 20, 30] then [40, 50, 60]. State its HWC shape and all three CHW planes. Give the green value at row 0 column 1 in both layouts. A batch contains four copies: give its NHWC shape and total channel-value count.
independent_case.answer: Teacher explanation: HWC shape is 1 by 2 by 3. CHW planes are [[10, 40]], [[20, 50]], [[30, 60]], giving shape 3 by 1 by 2. hwc[0][1][1] and chw[1][0][1] both equal 50. Batch shape is 4 by 1 by 2 by 3, containing 24 values.
independent_case.source: primary source W4, first curriculum occurrence

misconceptions: Channels are component planes at matching spatial positions in one image.
Reshaping automatically changes axis meanings correctly
Axis permutation must preserve coordinate correspondence; regrouping a flattened list can mix positions and colours.
Every conversion to a smaller number preserves information
Exact fixed scaling differs from rounding and channel averaging, which can collapse distinct values.

blocks.text: A channel-first layout uses image[channel][row][column], abbreviated CHW. Our image then has shape 3 by 2 by 2. A correct conversion preserves the rule chw[c][r][k] = hwc[r][k][c]. The code assumes a nonempty rectangular image with exactly three values per pixel.

blocks.title: Optional Python check
blocks.text:
hwc = [
    [[255, 0, 0], [0, 255, 0]],
    [[0, 0, 255], [255, 255, 255]],
]
height, width = len(hwc), len(hwc[0])
chw = [[[hwc[r][k][c] for k in range(width)]
        for r in range(height)] for c in range(3)]
for channel in chw:
    print(channel)
assert chw[2][1][0] == hwc[1][0][2] == 255
restored = [[[chw[c][r][k] for c in range(3)]
             for k in range(width)] for r in range(height)]
assert restored == hwc

Reading nested values in order and merely regrouping them into a new shape does not perform this axis conversion. The first four flattened HWC values are [255, 0, 0, 0]. A naive regrouping makes these the first channel plane, but the correct red plane is [[255, 0], [0, 255]]. Shape agreement alone cannot detect this mistake.
